script.title: When Phineas Gage Survived an Iron Rod Through His Head 🤯
script.hook_text: An iron rod pierced his head
sentences: In 1848, an iron rod blasted through Phineas Gage's head.
The Vermont railroad foreman was tamping explosives into rock with a custom tool.
A spark ignited the powder, rocketing the thirteen-pound iron bar right through his skull.
The rod landed eighty feet away while Phineas sat upright in an oxcart.
Sitting outside a hotel, he calmly told Doctor Williams he had business for him.
Williams thought Phineas was deceived until he saw the top of his head.
Phineas survived the blow and lived for twelve more years.
How much of a person remains when their brain loses a piece?
script.description:
The improbable survival of railroad foreman Phineas Gage after a blasting accident in 1848.
His case changed how science understood the human mind.

claims_en: In 1848 an iron rod passed through Phineas Gage's head during a railroad blasting accident in Cavendish, Vermont.
Phineas Gage was a railroad construction foreman tamping explosives with a custom iron rod.
The iron bar weighed thirteen and a quarter pounds and was propelled by an accidental explosion.
The tamping iron landed about eighty feet away, and Gage sat upright in an oxcart shortly after.
Gage greeted physician Edward H. Williams outside a hotel, saying the doctor had business enough for him.
Doctor Williams initially did not believe Gage's statement until examining the wound at the top of his skull.
Phineas Gage survived the accident and lived for another twelve years.
Gage's case influenced 19th-century discussions about brain function and personality.
